# Overview {.unnumbered}

{{< include _caution.qmd >}}

Yang's Tolerance Principle [@yang2005; @yang2016] says that a rule which could apply to $N$ items is productive only if its exceptions $e$ satisfy

$$
e \le \theta_N = \frac{N}{\ln N}.
$$

It is a strong claim. It is stricter than majority rule once $N$ exceeds about 8, and the tolerated *proportion* of exceptions, $1/\ln N$, keeps shrinking as the class grows: about 46% at $N = 9$, 22% at $N = 100$, 14% at $N = 1{,}000$.

The principle is usually derived from a model of real-time lexical processing. This book asks two questions about that derivation.

1. Does the derivation hold up on its own terms?
2. Is there an independent rational analysis, of learning, inference or storage, that yields the same threshold?

## Short answers

1. **The derivation is fragile.** The threshold follows from a serial-search cost model only if exceptions are no more frequent than regular items. When exceptions are frequent, as they are in English, the same cost model tolerates far more than $N/\ln N$ (@sec-derivation).
2. **Most rational analyses do not produce it.** A learner minimizing errors never has a reason to reject a rule (@sec-learnability). Bayesian model comparison and optimal description length give a threshold that is a constant proportion of $N$ (@sec-bayes, @sec-mdl). A storage-versus-computation model in the style of Fragment Grammars is far more permissive still (@sec-fragment).
3. **One structural assumption does produce it.** $N/\ln N$ appears whenever each exception carries its own fixed cost of about $\ln N$ that is not shared with the other exceptions: a step in a serial search, a full address in memory, or a separate surprise under a prior that says rules have about one exception. Wherever the cost of exceptions can be pooled, the logarithm disappears (@sec-synthesis).

## Chapters

| Chapter | Question | Result |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-derivation | What is Yang's derivation, and how robust is it? | Gives $N/\ln N$ only for frequency-neutral exceptions |
| @sec-learnability | Does an error-minimizing learner under Zipfian input need a threshold? | No: a rule with memorized exceptions never loses |
| @sec-bayes | Does Bayesian comparison of "rule" and "no rule" give it? | Only with a fixed prior of about one exception per rule |
| @sec-fragment | What does a storage-versus-computation model predict? | The rule survives almost any number of exceptions |
| @sec-mdl | What does optimal description length predict? | A constant proportion; $N/\ln N$ needs an ordered list of named exceptions |
| @sec-synthesis | What do the positive cases share, and what do the data require? | Unshared exception costs; the data do not pin down the functional form |

## Notation

Used throughout:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $N$ | number of item types the rule could apply to |
| $e$ | number of those items that are exceptions |
| $x = e/N$ | proportion of exceptions |
| $\theta_N = N/\ln N$ | the tolerance threshold |
| $H_N = \sum_{i=1}^{N} 1/i$ | the $N$th harmonic number, $\approx \ln N + 0.577$ |
| $p_i = 1/(i\,H_N)$ | Zipfian probability of the item at frequency rank $i$ |
| $S$ | number of tokens the learner has heard |
| $K$ | number of possible forms an item could take |
| $c$ | cost in nats of storing one form ($c = \ln K$ when forms are equiprobable) |

All costs are in nats. Every table and figure is computed in the chapter from the code in `sims/`.
